edo-period.name: Edo period
edo-period.summary: Japan's era of rule by the Tokugawa shogunate from 1600 to 1868, marked by long peace, strict social order, urban growth, and near-total isolation from the outside world.

history-of-sushi.name: Haya-zushi
history-of-sushi.summary: Part of the Edo-period (1603–1867) shift in sushi-making, when vinegar began to replace fermented rice, making sushi much faster to prepare.

ryukyu-islands.name: Ryukyu Islands
ryukyu-islands.summary: A chain of Japanese islands stretching from Kyushu to Taiwan, divided between Kagoshima and Okinawa prefectures, with Okinawa Island as the largest.

sakoku.name: Sakoku
sakoku.summary: Isolationist foreign policy of Japan's Tokugawa shogunate during the Edo period (1603 to 1868), severely restricting foreign trade and travel and enacted through edicts from 1633 to 1639.

tokugawa-yoshimune.name: Tokugawa Yoshimune
tokugawa-yoshimune.summary: Eighth shogun of the Tokugawa shogunate (r. 1716-1745), great-grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu, known for repealing the ban on Western literature.

fujian.name: Fujian
fujian.summary: A province in southeast China facing Taiwan across the strait, known for its linguistic diversity including several Min Chinese dialects.

castella.name: Castella
castella.summary: A moist, sweet Japanese sponge cake based on cakes Portuguese merchants introduced in the 16th century, later popularized in Nagasaki as a Japanese confectionery.

amami-shima.name: Amami Ōshima
amami-shima.summary: The largest island in Japan's Amami archipelago, between Kyūshū and Okinawa, home to about 73,000 people, much of it within a national park.

wasanbon.name: Wasanbon
wasanbon.summary: A fine-grained Japanese sugar traditionally made in Shikoku since about the 1770s, prized for use in wagashi sweets.

wagashi.name: Wagashi
wagashi.summary: Traditional Japanese confectionery made mainly from plant-based ingredients using pre-Western cooking methods, often served with green tea; most modern forms developed in the Edo period (1603-1868).

makisu.name: Makisu
makisu.summary: Small bamboo and cotton-string mat used in Japanese cooking to roll sushi such as makizushi and to shape foods like rolled omelettes.

dosirak.name: Dosirak
dosirak.summary: A Korean packed meal of rice and side dishes, whose name comes from an 18th-century word; it is homemade or sold in shops and stations.

joseon.name: Joseon
joseon.summary: A Korean dynastic kingdom founded in 1392 by Taejo, lasting 505 years until 1897, which entrenched Confucian ideals and saw the height of classical Korean culture and science.

meiji-era.name: Meiji era
meiji-era.summary: Period of Japanese history (1868–1912) under Emperor Meiji, when Japan moved from an isolated feudal society to a modern, industrialized world power.

norimaki.name: Norimaki
norimaki.summary: A Japanese term for foods wrapped in nori seaweed, most commonly referring to makizushi, or rolled sushi.

ukiyo-e.name: Ukiyo-e
ukiyo-e.summary: A genre of Japanese woodblock prints and paintings, flourishing from the 17th through 19th centuries, depicting beauties, kabuki actors, and the 'floating world' of pleasure districts.

suzuki-harunobu.name: Suzuki Harunobu
suzuki-harunobu.summary: Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock print artist (c. 1725-1770) who in 1765 became the first to produce full-color prints, making earlier two- and three-color methods obsolete.

katsura-imperial-villa.name: Katsura Imperial Villa
katsura-imperial-villa.summary: An Imperial residence with gardens in Kyoto, Japan, regarded as a notable example of traditional Japanese garden design.

nikk-t-sh-g.name: Nikkō Tōshō-gū
nikk-t-sh-g.summary: A Shinto shrine in Nikkō, Japan, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with several of its structures designated National Treasures of Japan.

nanban-art.name: Nanban art
nanban-art.summary: Japanese art shaped by contact with Portuguese and other European traders and missionaries from 1543, including folding screens showing foreigners in Japanese ports and towns.

nanban-trade.name: Nanban
nanban-trade.summary: A term originally for peoples of South Asia and Southeast Asia that came to mean the Portuguese and other Europeans arriving in Japan from 1543, naming the era's trade and art.

kan-school.name: Kanō school
kan-school.summary: The dominant Japanese painting school from the late 15th century until 1868, blending Chinese influence with a distinctively Japanese style and enjoying shogunate patronage.

tosa-school.name: Tosa school
tosa-school.summary: School of Japanese painting founded in the early Muromachi period, devoted to the yamato-e style of flat colour and precise outlines, in contrast to Chinese-influenced schools like Kanō.

oda-nobunaga.name: Oda Nobunaga
oda-nobunaga.summary: Japanese samurai and daimyō (1534–1582) regarded as the first of Japan's three great unifiers, noted for innovative military tactics and consolidating power over most of Honshu by 1580.

toyotomi-hideyoshi.name: Toyotomi Hideyoshi
toyotomi-hideyoshi.summary: Japanese samurai and daimyō (1537–1598) who rose from a peasant background to become the second 'Great Unifier' of Japan, attaining the titles of Imperial Regent and Chancellor.

azuchi-castle.name: Azuchi Castle
azuchi-castle.summary: One of Oda Nobunaga's primary castles, built 1576–1579 by Lake Biwa to watch over Kyoto; it was demolished in 1582 after Nobunaga's assassination.

fushimi-castle.name: Fushimi Castle (Momoyama Castle)
fushimi-castle.summary: Also called Momoyama Castle, it was built near Kyoto from 1592 to 1594 by Toyotomi Hideyoshi as his retirement residence and gave its name to the Azuchi–Momoyama period.

tenshu.name: Tenshu
tenshu.summary: The tallest tower and main keep within a Japanese castle complex, built of timber on stone foundations, a distinct style that emerged in the 1560s and 1570s.

nin-war.name: Ōnin War
nin-war.summary: A civil war in Japan from 1467 to 1477, sparked by a dispute between Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen, that drew in the Ashikaga shogunate and many feudal lords and began the long Sengoku 'Warring States' period.

sukiya-zukuri.name: Sukiya-zukuri
sukiya-zukuri.summary: Japanese residential architectural style rooted in tea house aesthetics, marked by natural materials, especially wood.

chashitsu.name: Chashitsu
chashitsu.summary: A Japanese architectural space designed for tea ceremony gatherings, typically featuring shoji screens, tatami floors, and a tokonoma alcove.

ry-tei.name: Ryōtei
ry-tei.summary: A traditional Japanese restaurant for discreet high-level business or political meetings, often featuring geisha entertainment, common until the 1960s.

azuchi-momoyama-period.name: Azuchi–Momoyama period
azuchi-momoyama-period.summary: The final phase of Japan's Sengoku period, 1568 to 1603, spanning Oda Nobunaga's rise and Toyotomi Hideyoshi's unification until the Tokugawa victory at Sekigahara.

torii-kiyonaga.name: Torii Kiyonaga
torii-kiyonaga.summary: Japanese ukiyo-e artist (1752–1815) who became head of the Torii school in 1787, known for elegant bijin-ga depictions of women and kabuki signboards.

utamaro.name: Utamaro
utamaro.summary: A Japanese ukiyo-e artist (c. 1753–1806) famed for his portraits of beautiful women, whose work later influenced Impressionist painters in France.

manila-galleon.name: Manila galleons
manila-galleon.summary: A Spanish trade route (1565–1815) linking the Philippines to Mexico across the Pacific, using galleons that made one or two round trips a year between Manila and Acapulco.

yi-sun-sin.name: Yi Sun-sin
yi-sun-sin.summary: A Korean admiral (1545-1598) famed for defeating the Japanese navy in at least 23 battles during the Imjin War, including a victory with 13 ships against over 130 at Myeongnyang, before dying in his final battle.

myeongnyang-strait.name: Myeongnyang Strait
myeongnyang-strait.summary: A narrow sea strait between mainland South Korea and Jindo Island in South Jeolla Province, also called Uldolmok, meaning 'screaming sea.'

battle-of-chilcheollyang.name: Battle of Chilcheollyang
battle-of-chilcheollyang.summary: A 1597 night naval battle of the Imjin War in which Japan's fleet destroyed nearly the entire Korean navy.

battle-of-nagashino.name: Battle of Nagashino
battle-of-nagashino.summary: An 1575 battle in which the allied forces of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu crushed the Takeda clan, seen as securing Nobunaga's path to unifying Japan.

tokugawa-ieyasu.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
tokugawa-ieyasu.summary: Founder and first shogun of the Tokugawa shogunate (1543-1616), one of Japan's three "Great Unifiers," who seized power after the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.

takeda-katsuyori.name: Takeda Katsuyori
takeda-katsuyori.summary: Japanese daimyō of the Sengoku period, head of the Takeda clan and successor to Takeda Shingen, who died in 1582.

tanegashima-gun.name: Tanegashima
tanegashima-gun.summary: Matchlock arquebus firearm introduced to Japan by the Portuguese in 1543, used by samurai and their ashigaru foot soldiers and credited with permanently changing Japanese warfare.

turtle-ship.name: turtle ship
turtle-ship.summary: A type of Korean warship used by the Joseon Navy from the early 15th into the 19th century, named for its shell-like covering and sometimes, uncertainly, described as an early ironclad.

nagashino-castle.name: Nagashino Castle
nagashino-castle.summary: A Sengoku-period Japanese castle and the site of the 1575 Battle of Nagashino, where Tokugawa Ieyasu and Oda Nobunaga fought Takeda Katsuyori.

t-d-takatora.name: Tōdō Takatora
t-d-takatora.summary: Japanese daimyō (1556 to 1630) who rose from a lowly foot soldier to a lord famed for castle design, credited with building around twenty castles including Edo Castle.

sword-hunt.name: Sword hunt
sword-hunt.summary: A campaign in Japanese history to confiscate weapons from potential rivals, most famously ordered by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1588.

separation-edict.name: Separation Edict
separation-edict.summary: A three-article law issued by Toyotomi Hideyoshi on 8 October 1591, fixing social status divisions in Japan.

wokou.name: Wokou
wokou.summary: Pirates known as 'Japanese pirates' or 'dwarf pirates' who raided the coasts of China and Korea from the 13th to 17th centuries, drawn from various East Asian peoples.

gifu.name: Gifu
gifu.summary: A city in central Japan that served as a strategic warlord base during the Sengoku period and was named by Oda Nobunaga.

battle-of-myeongnyang.name: Battle of Myeongnyang
battle-of-myeongnyang.summary: A 26 October 1597 battle in which Admiral Yi Sun-sin's outnumbered Joseon fleet sank or crippled 31 Japanese warships in the Myeongnyang Strait, a humiliating defeat for Japan.

imjin-war.name: Imjin War
imjin-war.summary: Two Japanese invasions of Korea, in 1592 and 1597, launched by Toyotomi Hideyoshi; the war ended in 1598 with Japan's withdrawal after Ming and Joseon forces halted the advance.

uesugi-kenshin.name: Uesugi Kenshin
uesugi-kenshin.summary: Japanese daimyō (1530 to 1578) known as the 'Dragon of Echigo,' a powerful Sengoku-period warlord famed for his military skill and long rivalry with Takeda Shingen.

takeda-shingen.name: Takeda Shingen
takeda-shingen.summary: Japanese samurai and daimyō of the Sengoku period known as the 'Tiger of Kai', one of the era's most powerful and esteemed military lords (1521–1573).

battles-of-kawanakajima.name: Kawanakajima
battles-of-kawanakajima.summary: A plain in Japan where rival warlords Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin fought five inconclusive battles between 1553 and 1564, later celebrated as an epitome of Japanese chivalry.

japanese-war-fan.name: Tessen
japanese-war-fan.summary: A folding hand fan used by samurai in feudal Japan as a weapon or for signalling, made in several distinct types.

matsuo-bash.name: Matsuo Bashō
matsuo-bash.summary: Japanese poet of the Edo period (1644–1694), regarded as the greatest master of haiku (then called hokku) and known for his travel essays.

hokku.name: hokku
hokku.summary: The opening stanza of a Japanese linked poem (renga or renku), later renamed 'haiku' by Masaoka Shiki when written as a standalone poem.

chikamatsu-monzaemon.name: Chikamatsu Monzaemon
chikamatsu-monzaemon.summary: A Japanese dramatist of jōruri puppet theater and kabuki, widely regarded as the greatest Japanese dramatist, famous for plays about the double-suicides of honor-bound lovers; he lived 1653–1725.

the-tale-of-the-heike.name: The Tale of the Heike
the-tale-of-the-heike.summary: An epic account, compiled before 1330, of the struggle between the Taira and Minamoto clans for control of Japan during the Genpei War (1180–1185); translated into English at least five times.

gasa-poetry.name: Gasa
gasa-poetry.summary: A Korean verse form popular during the Joseon period, commonly sung and especially popular among yangban women, perfected by the 16th-century poet Chŏng Ch'ŏl.

yangban.name: Yangban
yangban.summary: The hereditary scholar-official aristocracy that ruled Joseon-era Korea, serving as government administrators overseeing its agrarian bureaucracy into the 20th century.

haikai.name: Haikai
haikai.summary: A genre of Japanese linked verse that developed in the 16th century from earlier aristocratic renga, known for satire and puns until Matsuo Bashō gave it a more serious tone.

oku-no-hosomichi.name: Oku no Hosomichi
oku-no-hosomichi.summary: A major haibun travel work by Japanese poet Matsuo Bashō, considered one of the classics of Japanese literature; first published posthumously in 1702.

motoori-norinaga.name: Motoori Norinaga
motoori-norinaga.summary: Japanese scholar (1730–1801) of the nativist Kokugaku movement during the Edo period, ranked among its Four Great Men.

waka-poetry.name: Waka (poetry)
waka-poetry.summary: A form of poetry in classical Japanese literature, also called yamato-uta, distinct from the Chinese-style kanshi verse.

kokugaku.name: Kokugaku
kokugaku.summary: An Edo-period Japanese scholarly movement that turned study away from Chinese, Confucian and Buddhist texts toward research into early Japanese classics.

hiraga-gennai.name: Hiraga Gennai
hiraga-gennai.summary: A Japanese polymath and rōnin of the Edo period (c. 1729–1779/80): a pharmacologist, Rangaku scholar, inventor of an electrostatic generator and thermometer, and author of satirical fiction.

rangaku.name: Rangaku
rangaku.summary: The body of Western scientific and technical knowledge Japan gained through contact with the Dutch enclave of Dejima while otherwise closed to foreigners, from 1641 to 1853.

sugita-genpaku.name: Sugita Genpaku
sugita-genpaku.summary: Japanese physician (1733–1817) who translated Kaitai Shinsho, a Dutch anatomy text, becoming a founder of Rangaku and Dutch-style medicine in Japan.

kaitai-shinsho.name: Kaitai Shinsho
kaitai-shinsho.summary: 1774 Japanese medical text by Sugita Genpaku, translated from a Dutch anatomy book and the first full translation of a Western-language work into Japanese.

later-jin-invasion-of-joseon.name: Later Jin invasion of Joseon
later-jin-invasion-of-joseon.summary: A brief 1627 invasion of Korea's Joseon Kingdom by the Later Jin, ending after three months with Joseon becoming a tributary of the Later Jin.

qing-invasion-of-joseon.name: Qing invasion of Joseon
qing-invasion-of-joseon.summary: 1636 invasion of Korea's Joseon Kingdom by the newly formed Manchu-led Qing Empire, which forced Joseon to break ties with the Ming dynasty and become a Qing tributary.

taejo-of-joseon.name: Taejo of Joseon
taejo-of-joseon.summary: Founder of the Joseon dynasty, who took the throne in 1392 after overthrowing Goryeo, ruled six years, and was later honored as Emperor Ko.

korean-empire.name: Korean Empire
korean-empire.summary: Korean monarchical state proclaimed in 1897 by King Gojong, marked by the modernizing Gwangmu Reform, ending with Japan's annexation of Korea in 1910.

neo-confucianism.name: Neo-Confucianism
neo-confucianism.summary: A revival of Confucianism as an ethical, social and religious system that dominated Chinese philosophy from the 13th to 19th century, developed under Zhu Xi during the Song dynasty.

tokugawa-shogunate.name: Tokugawa shogunate
tokugawa-shogunate.summary: Japan's military government from 1603 to 1868, founded by Tokugawa Ieyasu; enforced isolationist policies and a strict class system until its overthrow in the 1868 Meiji Restoration.

kakure-kirishitan.name: Kakure Kirishitan
kakure-kirishitan.summary: Japanese Catholics who went underground after Christianity was repressed by the Tokugawa shogunate in the early 17th century, secretly preserving their faith until the ban was lifted in 1873.

daimyo.name: Daimyō
daimyo.summary: Powerful Japanese feudal lords who, from the 15th century to the mid-19th century, ruled most of Japan from vast hereditary landholdings while remaining subordinate to the shogun.

nagasaki-bugy.name: Nagasaki bugyō
nagasaki-bugy.summary: Officials of the Tokugawa shogunate in Edo-period Japan holding a senior administrative post, usually but not always given to daimyōs.

gwanghaegun-of-joseon.name: Gwanghaegun of Joseon
gwanghaegun-of-joseon.summary: 15th monarch of Joseon (r. 1608–1623), later deposed in a coup led by his nephew, who reigned as King Injo.

nurhaci.name: Nurhaci
nurhaci.summary: Founding khan of the Later Jin dynasty (1559–1626) who united the Jurchen tribes, built the Eight Banners military system, and is credited with creating a Manchu writing script.

battle-of-sekigahara.name: Battle of Sekigahara
battle-of-sekigahara.summary: A decisive 1600 battle in which Tokugawa Ieyasu's forces defeated a coalition loyal to the Toyotomi clan, marking the start of the Tokugawa shogunate that ruled Japan until 1868.

r-nin.name: Rōnin
r-nin.summary: A samurai left without a lord or master, typically after the lord's death or loss of favor, in Japan between 1185 and 1868.

ayutthaya-kingdom.name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
ayutthaya-kingdom.summary: A Thai kingdom centered on the city of Ayutthaya from 1351 to 1767, a major hub of international trade considered a precursor of modern Thailand.

toungoo-dynasty.name: Toungoo dynasty
toungoo-dynasty.summary: Ruling dynasty of Burma from the mid-16th century to 1752, at its peak considered probably the largest empire in Southeast Asian history, spanning from Assam to Cambodia.

hyeonjong-of-joseon.name: Hyeonjong of Joseon
hyeonjong-of-joseon.summary: 18th monarch of Joseon, 1641 to 1674, whose reign was marked by factional conflict over funeral rites; the only Joseon king who took no concubines.

hendrick-hamel.name: Hendrick Hamel
hendrick-hamel.summary: Dutch sailor (1630 to after 1692) shipwrecked off Jeju Island in 1653; after 13 years in Joseon Korea he wrote the first Western account of the country.

hayashi-razan.name: Hayashi Razan
hayashi-razan.summary: Japanese historian, philosopher and writer (1583–1657) who tutored and advised the first four Tokugawa shoguns and founded the Hayashi clan of Confucian scholars.

arai-hakuseki.name: Arai Hakuseki
arai-hakuseki.summary: Confucianist scholar-bureaucrat, writer and politician in Japan's Edo period (1657–1725) who advised the shōgun Tokugawa Ienobu.

seonbi.name: Seonbi
seonbi.summary: Scholars of the Goryeo and Joseon periods who, though often of noble background, gave up wealth and power for lives of study, seen as models of intelligence, morality and composure.

zhu-xi.name: Zhu Xi
zhu-xi.summary: A Chinese philosopher, historian and politician (1130–1200) of the Southern Song dynasty, the leading figure of Neo-Confucianism, whose commentaries were core exam texts until 1905.

wang-yangming.name: Wang Yangming
wang-yangming.summary: Ming dynasty Chinese statesman, general and Neo-Confucian philosopher (1472–1529), regarded as the most important Neo-Confucian thinker after Zhu Xi and founder of the Lu–Wang school of thought.

silhak.name: Silhak
silhak.summary: A Korean Confucian reform movement of the late Joseon dynasty promoting practical, empirical approaches to society, land reform and science over rigid tradition.

matteo-ricci.name: Matteo Ricci
matteo-ricci.summary: Italian Jesuit missionary (1552–1610) at the Ming court who mastered Chinese and became the first European to enter Beijing's Forbidden City.

amakusa-kumamoto.name: Amakusa
amakusa-kumamoto.summary: A city in Kumamoto Prefecture, Japan, with an estimated population of about 72,000 people spread over roughly 684 square kilometres.

ishin-s-den.name: Ishin Sūden
ishin-s-den.summary: A Japanese Rinzai Zen monk (1569–1633) who advised shoguns Tokugawa Ieyasu, Hidetada and Iemitsu on religious and foreign affairs, shaping the early Tokugawa shogunate.

tokugawa-hidetada.name: Tokugawa Hidetada
tokugawa-hidetada.summary: Second shogun of the Tokugawa dynasty (r. 1605-1623), son of Tokugawa Ieyasu and maternal grandfather of Empress Meishō.

yi-s-nghun.name: Yi Sŭnghun
yi-s-nghun.summary: A Korean Catholic missionary (1756-1801), baptized as Peter, considered one of the first Christians and martyrs in Korea.

sencha.name: Sencha
sencha.summary: A Japanese green tea made by infusing whole processed leaves in hot water, unlike powdered matcha; it is the most popular tea in Japan.

francis-xavier.name: Francis Xavier
francis-xavier.summary: Navarrese cleric and missionary (1506–1552) who co-founded the Society of Jesus and led the first Christian mission to Japan, also spreading Christianity across Asia and Portuguese India.

cosme-de-torres.name: Cosme de Torres
cosme-de-torres.summary: Spanish Jesuit from Valencia (1510-1570) and one of the first Christian missionaries in Japan, where he died.

juan-fern-ndez-missionary.name: Juan Fernández
juan-fern-ndez-missionary.summary: Spanish Jesuit lay brother and missionary (1526?–1567) who became the first European to write a grammar and lexicon of the Japanese language.

anjir.name: Anjirō
anjir.summary: The first recorded Japanese Christian, who fled Japan after a killing, met Francis Xavier in Portuguese Malacca, and returned to Japan with him as interpreter for the first Jesuit mission to Japan.

ukita-hideie.name: Ukita Hideie
ukita-hideie.summary: A Japanese samurai and daimyō of Bizen and Mimasaka Provinces, one of the Five Elders appointed by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, exiled after fighting Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara.

gyeongbokgung.name: Gyeongbokgung
gyeongbokgung.summary: The first royal palace of Korea's Joseon dynasty, built in Seoul in 1395, burned in 1592, and largely demolished under Japanese colonial rule before later restoration.

sen-no-riky.name: Sen no Rikyū
sen-no-riky.summary: A Japanese tea master, 1522 to 1591, seen as the most important influence on the tea ceremony, especially its rustic simplicity, whose descendants founded the three schools still teaching his tradition.

takeno-j.name: Takeno Jōō
takeno-j.summary: Tea ceremony master and merchant in 16th-century Japan who developed the wabi-cha style and taught Sen no Rikyū (1502–1555).

sakai.name: Sakai
sakai.summary: City in Osaka Prefecture, Japan, one of the country's most important seaports since medieval times and known for its kofun burial mounds and cutlery.

26-martyrs-of-japan.name: 26 Martyrs of Japan
26-martyrs-of-japan.summary: Group of Catholics executed by crucifixion in Nagasaki on 5 February 1597, a landmark event in the suppression of Christianity in Japan.

uchi-yoshitaka.name: Ōuchi Yoshitaka
uchi-yoshitaka.summary: A Japanese daimyō (1507–1551) who led the Ōuchi clan and fought rival clans for control of Aki and Kyūshū, later turning to arts and foreign trade and hosting the missionary Francis Xavier in his capital, Yamaguchi.

kaiseki.name: Kaiseki
kaiseki.summary: Traditional multi-course Japanese meal, either a formal set banquet or the simple meal served before a tea ceremony (cha-kaiseki).

wabi-sabi.name: Wabi-sabi
wabi-sabi.summary: A traditional Japanese aesthetic centered on accepting transience and imperfection, valuing austere, subdued beauty (wabi) and the rustic patina of aged things (sabi).

iemoto.name: Iemoto
iemoto.summary: A Japanese term for the founder or current Grand Master of a school of traditional Japanese art, such as tea ceremony or calligraphy, within a hierarchical, family-based system.

emperor-go-y-zei.name: Emperor Go-Yōzei
emperor-go-y-zei.summary: 107th emperor of Japan (1571–1617), reigning from 1586 until his abdication in 1611, spanning the transition from the Azuchi–Momoyama period to the Edo period.

classic-of-filial-piety.name: Classic of Filial Piety
classic-of-filial-piety.summary: A Confucian text on how to behave towards elders and rulers, likely written in the late Warring States or early Han period as a dialogue with Confucius, widely used to teach children.

nihon-shoki.name: Nihon Shoki
nihon-shoki.summary: The second-oldest book of classical Japanese history, completed in 720, giving the most complete surviving record of ancient Japan from myth through the 8th century.
